title: Live-cell FRET imaging-based efficacy prediction of EGFR-TKIs in EGFR L858R-mutant NSCLC.
abstract: Functional assays can assist individualised selection of treatment regimens by evaluating the ex vivo response of tumour cells to anticancer therapeutics.
However, the two major strategies used to assess responses to targeted drugs, target-based profiling and phenotypic profiling, have inherent limitations.
Target-based profiling does not directly capture downstream cell-fate outcomes, whereas phenotypic profiling provides limited mechanistic information on drug action.

Live-cell fluorescence resonance energy transfer (FRET) microscopy was used to integrate the interaction between EGFR L858R and GRB2 with cellular phenotypic features, thereby predicting the efficacy of EGFR-tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) at the single-cell level.

The target-based drug score (T-score), derived from the interaction between EGFR L858R and GRB2 in living cells co-expressing CFP-EGFR L858R and YFP-GRB2, enabled evaluation of the on-target activity of EGFR-TKIs against EGFR L858R .
The phenotype drug score (P-score), constructed from cellular phenotype features, characterised the phenotypic responses induced by EGFR-TKIs.
The TP-score, integrating the T- and P-scores, accurately predicted the efficacy of EGFR-TKIs.
In living H3255 cells, the TP-score of osimertinib (OSI) was higher than that of gefitinib (GEF).
Notably, in H3255 cell-derived xenograft (CDX) mouse models, OSI showed superior in vivo antitumour efficacy compared with GEF.

Furthermore, live-cell TP scoring revealed that primary tumour cells from a patient with NSCLC did not respond to OSI, a finding consistent with the absence of actionable EGFR mutations in this patient.
This study demonstrates the clinical feasibility of predicting EGFR-TKI efficacy by integrating EGFR L858R -GRB2 interactions with cellular phenotypic features in single living cells.

body.text: A central challenge in clinical precision oncology is matching individual patients with the most effective therapeutic agents.
Precision oncology currently relies primarily on genomic sequencing to identify patient-specific genetic alterations and guide targeted therapy selection.
However, the clinical benefit of genomics-guided therapy remains limited.
The rate of successful drug matching is approximately 10%, and the objective response rate (ORR) among matched patients generally does not exceed 20%.
Patients with identical mutations often exhibit different sensitivities to targeted therapies.
For EGFR L858R-mutant non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), more than ten first- to third-generation EGFR-TKIs have been approved.
EGFR-TKIs inhibit EGFR kinase activity and downstream signalling pathways to suppress tumour growth.

First-generation TKIs, such as gefitinib (GEF) and erlotinib, reversibly bind to the ATP-binding pocket of EGFR, whereas second-generation TKIs, such as afatinib (AFA) and dacomitinib, form irreversible covalent bonds with EGFR.
Third-generation TKIs, such as osimertinib (OSI), selectively and irreversibly target mutant EGFR harbouring sensitising mutations and the T790M resistance mutation.

A network meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials in advanced EGFR L858R-mutant NSCLC found that no first-line EGFR-TKI demonstrated an overall survival (OS) advantage over other first-line EGFR-TKIs.
However, Shimbu et al. reported substantial interindividual variability in sensitivity to different EGFR-TKIs among patients with EGFR L858R-mutant NSCLC.
These findings suggest that population-level evidence may be insufficient to identify the optimal therapy for individual patients.

As a complementary approach to guiding cancer therapy,, ex vivo functional assays for targeted drugs primarily employ two drug screening strategies: assessing drug-induced changes in target activity and phenotypic responses in tumour samples.

Drug target profiling techniques, such as single-molecule pull-down and co-immunoprecipitation (SMPC), kinase activity profiling using peptide arrays, and liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) assays, frequently rely on the analysis of dead cancer cells, , , and often fail to reliably predict downstream biological effects.

Using an LC-MS/MS assay, Gosline et al. reported that FLT3 expression and phosphorylation did not correlate significantly with ex vivo cell viability responses to the FLT3 inhibitor quizartinib in samples from 38 patients with acute myeloid leukaemia (AML).

Conversely, phenotypic profiling can capture drug-induced cellular outcomes, but it cannot determine whether the observed responses are mediated by the intended drug target, particularly in the presence of off-target effects., , , Zhai et al. found that tumour cells from a patient with liver cancer exhibited more than 50% viability inhibition in response to the multi-target TKI sorafenib using a digital microfluidic drug screening platform.
However, subsequent whole-exome sequencing revealed no mutations in sorafenib-targeted genes.
Live-cell fluorescence resonance energy transfer (FRET) imaging and high-content screening (HCS) have both been applied to drug screening.
FRET imaging enables real-time monitoring of protein-protein interactions (PPIs) in living cells and can be used to assess drug-induced changes in target activity.
In 1995, Lee et al. employed FRET to rapidly screen for novel HIV-1 integrase inhibitors to facilitate antiviral agent development.

In recent decades, FRET-based screening methods have expanded in drug discovery to encompass additional compound classes, such as anticancer agents, G protein-coupled receptor modulators, membrane-potential modulators, antiparasitic drugs, and Ca2+-signalling modulators.

For clinical applications, Mizutani et al. developed a FRET-based biosensor to predict the clinical efficacy of BCR-ABL TKIs in patients with chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML) by measuring BCR-ABL kinase activity in ex vivo bone marrow mononuclear cells., , HCS captures multiparametric morphological features and identifies complex phenotypic alterations without prior assumptions, thereby characterising cellular responses to drug treatments.
Initially developed in the mid-1990s as a novel drug discovery tool, HCS has since been extensively applied in drug development, functional genomics, and fundamental biological research.

Previous reports indicated that more than six commercial automated HCS microscopy platforms and more than 20 open-source or commercial image-analysis software packages were available., In the last decade, the use of HCS in precision oncology has steadily expanded., , , For example, Oh et al. employed HCS on tumour cells from 12 glioblastoma patients, identifying one patient whose tumour cells were sensitive to MET-TKIs.
Similarly, in a single-arm, open-label study, Kornauth et al. used single-cell HCS to guide treatment decisions in patients with advanced, aggressive hematologic cancers.

Among patients whose treatment was guided by HCS, 54% experienced more than a 1.3-fold improvement in progression-free survival (PFS) compared with prior therapy, and 40% achieved at least a threefold extension of absolute PFS relative to the expected median.
Live-cell FRET microscopy enables simultaneous analysis of EGFRL858R-GRB2 interactions and cellular phenotypic changes at the single-cell level.
EGFR primarily activates RAS-MAPK, PI3K-AKT, and JAK/STAT signalling, with GRB2 recruitment directly contributing to the RAS-MAPK and PI3K-AKT pathways.

EGFR-TKIs reduce the EGFR-GRB2 interaction, and downstream signalling,, and these effects can alter mitochondrial morphology, promote apoptosis, and suppress proliferation., Live-cell FRET microscopy can quantify the EGFR-TKI-induced reduction in the EGFR-GRB2 interaction, and can also reveal EGFR-TKI-induced morphological changes, such as changes in cell size and cell roundness.

In this study, we integrated live-cell FRET microscopy-based analyses of both EGFRL858R-GRB2 interactions and cellular phenotypes to predict the efficacy of EGFR-TKIs in H3255 cells (an EGFR L858R-mutant NSCLC cell line) and the clinical efficacy of OSI in primary tumour cells from an NSCLC patient.
We quantified EGFRL858R-GRB2 interactions using live-cell FRET imaging in cells co-expressing CFP-EGFRL858R and YFP-GRB2, deriving a target-based drug score (T-score).
Additionally, phenotypic features extracted from bright-field (BF) and mitochondrial (MITO) fluorescence images were used to calculate a phenotype-based drug score (P-score).
The combined T- and P-scores formed an integrated TP-score, which served as the final predictor of drug efficacy.
In H3255 cells co-expressing CFP-EGFRL858R and YFP-GRB2, the TP-score for OSI was higher than that for GEF, consistent with findings from H3255 CDX models.
Furthermore, live-cell TP scoring prospectively predicted primary insensitivity to OSI in a patient with NSCLC.
Figure 1 presents the schematic workflow of live-cell TP scoring, including sample preparation, data acquisition, and data analysis for drug efficacy evaluation.

Protein-protein interaction networks were generated using the STRING v12.5 database (https://string-db.org/) with the following settings: network type, physical subnetwork; meaning of network edges, confidence; active interaction sources, text mining, experiments, and databases; and minimum required interaction score, 0.900.
KEGG pathway enrichment analyses were also performed using STRING (FDR ≤ 0.05).

Correlation analyses of gene expression utilised GEPIA2 (http://gepia2.cancer-pku.cn/) based on TCGA (https://www.cancer.gov/ccg/research/genome-sequencing/tcga) lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) data (n = 483), with Pearson's correlation coefficient.

Gene expression levels in LUAD tumours and normal tissues from TCGA (tumour, n = 483; normal, n = 59) and GTEx (https://www.genome.gov/Funded-Programs-Projects/Genotype-Tissue-Expression-Project, normal, n = 288) were analysed using GEPIA2.

Differences in OS and PFS between high- and low-expression groups were assessed using the ‘Expression & Survival’ module of GSCA (https://guolab.wchscu.cn/GSCA) based on TCGA LUAD data (tumour, n = 517; normal, n = 59; paired samples, n = 58).
Correlations between gene expression and sensitivity to GEF and AFA across pan-cancer data were also examined through GSCA, utilising the GDSC database (https://www.cancerrxgene.org/).
The NCI-H3255 cell line was purchased from Meisen Chinese Tissue Culture Collection.
Primary tumour cells were isolated from LUAD patient samples.
Cells were maintained in RPMI 1640 medium supplemented with 15% FBS and cultured at 37°C in a humidified incubator containing 5% CO2.
Cells were seeded in 15-mm glass-bottom dishes before transfection.
H3255 cells were transfected with plasmids using LipofectamineTM 3000 according to the manufacturer's instructions.
For FRET experiments, CFP-EGFRL858R and YFP-GRB2 plasmids were mixed at ratios of 1:1 or 1:2 and co-transfected into the same dish.
The total plasmid DNA per dish was 1000 ng.
Primary tumour cells were transfected with mRNA using LipofectamineTM MessengerMAXTM according to the manufacturer's protocol.
CFP-EGFRL858R and YFP-GRB2 mRNA complexes were transfected at a 3:1 ratio, totalling 600 ng per dish.
Cells were washed once with PBS, stained with 100 μM MitoTracker Deep Red 633, and incubated at 37°C in a 5% CO2 incubator for 20 min according to the manufacturer's protocol.
Cells were then washed three times with PBS and imaged by fluorescence microscopy.
FRET microscopy was performed using an Apotome 2 widefield microscope (Olympus, Japan) to acquire three-channel FRET images (DD, DA, AA), BF images, and MITO fluorescence images.
The imaging system configuration was described previously.,
Quantitative FRET analysis was performed as previously described., Briefly, regions of interests (ROIs) were selected from CFP-EGFRL858R-enriched areas in three-channel FRET images.
The donor-centric FRET efficiency (ED ) and acceptor-donor ratio (RC ) were calculated for each ROI.
To generate ED -RC binding curves, ED values were binned according to RC concentration ratios.
Mean ED values for each bin were plotted against RC , and the resulting curves were fitted using Origin 64 software.

Formulas employed were previously published., For each drug-treated ROI, Ti was calculated using the following equation (Equation 1): (1) Ti=xidrug-xcontrol ̄ where xidrug is the ED of the ith drug-treated ROI, and xcontrol ̄ represents the mean ED of control ROIs.
The final T-score was defined as the mean Ti across all drug-treated ROIs and calculated as: (2) T=1n∑i=1nTi where n denotes the total number of drug-treated ROIs.
Single-cell masks were generated from BF images and MITO fluorescence images using the Cellpose model.

CellProfiler was then used to extract BF features (AreaShape, Texture) and MITO features (AreaShape, Texture, Neighbours, RadialDistribution, Granularity, Intensity) from the single-cell phenotype regions identified by these masks.
Linear discriminant analysis (LDA) was performed to calculate the phenotype-based (P) score, combining both categories of single-cell features.
For each drug-treated group, data from treated cells and matched control cells were split into training and test sets (ratio 7:3) for LDA model training.
For each drug-treated cell (i) in the test set, the phenotype change score (Pi ) was computed from the LDA output probabilities as follows: (3) Pi=LDAy=drug|xd,itest-LDAy=drug|xctest ̄

Here, LDA(y=drug|xd,itest) represents the probability from the LDA model that the ith drug-treated test cell is classified as drug-treated, and LDA(y=drug|xctest) ̄ is the average LDA probability of control test cells classified as drug-treated.
The final P-score is the mean Pi across all drug-treated cells: (4) P=1n∑i=1nPi where n denotes the number of drug-treated cells.
Using the T-score (Equation 2) and P-score (Equation 4), the integrated TP-score was calculated as follows: (5) TP=10×[(T+1)P-1]
A higher TP-score, reflecting substantial on-target activity and notable phenotypic responses, indicates greater drug efficacy according to this evaluation system.
For multi-drug comparisons, P-, T-, and TP-scores were normalised on a scale from 0 to 1, where control = 0 and the highest-scoring drug = 1.
Cell viability was assessed using CCK-8.
Cells were seeded into 96-well plates, exposed to the indicated drugs, and incubated for 48 h.
Subsequently, 100 μL of serum-free RPMI 1640 medium containing 10% CCK-8 reagent was added to each well, followed by incubation for 1 h.
Absorbance at 450 nm was measured using a microplate reader.
Cells (1 × 103 per well) were seeded in 6-well plates and treated with the indicated drugs on the following day.
After 14 days, cells were washed with cold PBS, fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde for 10 min, and stained with crystal violet solution for 10 min.
When cultures in 6-well plates reached approximately 90% confluence, a scratch was made using a 200 μL pipette tip.
Microscopy images of the scratch areas were acquired at 0 and 24 h post-treatment, and scratch closure was quantified using Fiji ImageJ.

The animal experiments were approved by the Laboratory Animal Welfare and Ethics Committee of Jinan University (Approval no. IACUC-20250905-04).
Female BALB/c nude mice (4-6 weeks old) received subcutaneous injections into the right axilla containing 1 × 107 stable H3255 cells suspended in 100 μL of serum-free medium with 50% Matrigel.
Tumour size was monitored every 3 days using calliper measurements, and tumour volume was calculated using the formula: Volume = 0.5 × (largest diameter) × (smallest diameter).
Mice were randomised into treatment groups when the mean initial tumour volume reached approximately 100-150 mm3.
Randomisation was performed to ensure comparable tumour volumes across groups.
Three treatment groups were established, with 5 mice per group.
Mice received daily oral gavage with vehicle control (saline), GEF (51.4 mg/kg), or OSI (16.4 mg/kg).
Tumour volume and body weight were recorded every 3 days during treatment.
After 21 days of treatment, mice were euthanised, and xenografts were excised, photographed, and weighed.
This study was approved by the Institutional Review Board of the First Affiliated Hospital of Jinan University (KY-2024-230) and conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.
Written informed consent was obtained from all patients.
Surgically resected tumour specimens were collected from patients with LUAD at the First Affiliated Hospital of Jinan University.

To evaluate the on-target activity of EGFR-TKIs against EGFR, we performed bioinformatic screening of EGFR-interacting proteins to identify suitable candidates for FRET biosensor development.
Upon activation, EGFR recruits multiple adaptor and signalling proteins to initiate downstream signalling cascades involving VAV2, CBL, GRB2, SHC1, PLCG1, NCK1, STAT1, STAT3, and PTK2.
To identify proteins serving as key mediators of EGFR-related signalling in NSCLC, we examined the relationships between EGFR and these signalling proteins.
First, a physical interaction network was constructed using the STRING database with the highest confidence threshold (0.9).
Strong physical associations were identified between EGFR and several proteins, including GRB2, CBL, SHC1, PLCG1, STAT3, and PTK2 (Figure 2A).

Among these proteins, GRB2 displayed strong physical associations with all examined signalling proteins except STAT3 and STAT5, whereas STAT3 exhibited the fewest associations among EGFR-interacting proteins (Figure 2A).
We next performed KEGG pathway enrichment analysis on EGFR and its physically associated proteins, including GRB2, CBL, SHC1, PLCG1, STAT3, and PTK2.
Gene sets containing EGFR together with GRB2, STAT3, or PLCG1 were significantly enriched in pathways associated with NSCLC and EGFR-TKI resistance (Figures 2B-D and S1A-C).
Because EGFR mutations in NSCLC occur predominantly in LUAD, subsequent analyses focused on GRB2, STAT3, and PLCG1 in this subtype.
Gene expression analysis in patients with LUAD showed that EGFR expression was positively correlated with GRB2 and PLCG1 expression (Figures 2E,F and S1D).
However, high PLCG1 expression was associated with prolonged OS and PFS (Figure 2G), and PLCG1 expression was significantly lower in LUAD tissues than in normal controls (Figure S1E).
These findings support the hypothesis that PLCG1 may participate in a negative feedback pathway that suppresses EGFR activation.
Nevertheless, previous studies have also suggested that PLCG1 activation may promote migration and invasion in EGFR-mutant NSCLC.

The dual and potentially opposing roles of PLCG1 indicate that the EGFR-PLCG1 interaction cannot reliably predict a consistent biological outcome, limiting its suitability for evaluating the on-target activity of EGFR-TKIs.
Collectively, these findings suggest that GRB2 acts as a central mediator of EGFR-driven pro-tumourigenic signalling in NSCLC.
KEGG pathway enrichment analysis further showed that EGFR and GRB2 were significantly enriched in pathways associated with EGFR-TKI resistance (Figure 2D).
To determine whether GRB2 expression was associated with EGFR-TKI resistance, we performed drug sensitivity analysis using GSCA based on the GDSC database.
GRB2 expression was positively correlated with resistance to GEF and AFA across pan-cancer datasets (Figure 2H).
In addition, GRB2 has previously been reported to enhance EGFR-TKI resistance in NSCLC.
Furthermore, EGFR-GRB2 colocalisation has been identified as a prognostic biomarker in LUAD.

Importantly, the EGFR-GRB2 interaction can be quantitatively detected using FRET technology., Therefore, the EGFR-GRB2 interaction was selected in this study to evaluate the on-target activity of EGFR-TKIs.

body.text: Initially, CellProfiler was used to extract BF (AreaShape, Texture) and MITO features (AreaShape, Texture, Neighbours, RadialDistribution, Granularity, Intensity) from single-cell masks.

body.section: P-score of OSI in living H3255 cells
body.text: The combined feature dataset was then divided into training and test sets at a ratio of 7:3, and an LDA classifier was trained using the training set.

body.section: P-score of OSI in living H3255 cells
body.text: The classifier achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.874 in the test set (Figure 4C), indicating robust discrimination between DMSO- and OSI-treated cells based on integrated BF and MITO features.

body.section: P-score of OSI in living H3255 cells
body.text: To assess the added value of feature integration, predicted probabilities were also calculated using BF-only and MITO-only features.

body.section: P-score of OSI in living H3255 cells
body.text: The combined BF and MITO feature set achieved superior separation compared with either feature set alone (Figure 4D).

body.section: P-score of OSI in living H3255 cells
body.text: Using this integrated approach, a statistically significant difference in predicted probability distributions was observed between DMSO- and OSI-treated cells (Figure 4E).

body.section: P-score of OSI in living H3255 cells
body.text: Accordingly, the P-score was defined as the mean difference in predicted probabilities between these two groups (Figure 4F).

body.section: P-score of OSI in living H3255 cells
body.text: The average predicted probabilities were 0.332 for DMSO-treated cells and 0.489 for OSI-treated cells, yielding a P-score of 0.157 for OSI.

body.section: P-score of OSI in living H3255 cells
body.text: These findings indicate that the P-score can quantitatively characterise OSI-induced cellular phenotypic responses.

body.section: TP-scores of EGFR-TKIs in living H3255 cells
body.text: According to Equation 5, OSI had a TP-score of 0.219, considerably higher than that of the control (0), demonstrating that the TP-score quantitatively represents OSI's efficacy.

body.section: TP-scores of EGFR-TKIs in living H3255 cells
body.text: We next applied TP scoring to predict the efficacy of three EGFR-TKIs (GEF, AFA, OSI), one ALK-TKI (ALE), and one chemotherapeutic drug (GEM) in H3255 cells.

body.section: TP-scores of EGFR-TKIs in living H3255 cells
body.text: Cells co-expressing CFP-EGFRL858R and YFP-GRB2 were treated with each drug for 16 h.

body.section: TP-scores of EGFR-TKIs in living H3255 cells
body.text: To approximate maximal in vivo tumour exposure, drug concentrations were set at their maximum plasma concentrations (C max) reported in patients receiving recommended clinical doses: GEF (0.356 μM), AFA (0.052 μM), OSI (0.126 μM), ALE (1.38 μM), and GEM (89.3 μM).

body.section: TP-scores of EGFR-TKIs in living H3255 cells
body.text: Using clinically relevant C max concentrations ensures the translational significance of TP-scores.

body.section: TP-scores of EGFR-TKIs in living H3255 cells
body.text: To confirm that these concentrations were appropriate for TP scoring, we first assessed the in vitro antitumour activities of the five drugs at their respective C max values in H3255 cells GEF, AFA, OSI, and GEM induced significant cytotoxicity (Figure S3A).

body.section: TP-scores of EGFR-TKIs in living H3255 cells
body.text: Additionally, all five drugs inhibited colony formation (Figure S3B) and reduced cell viability (Figure S3C).

body.section: TP-scores of EGFR-TKIs in living H3255 cells
body.text: GEF, AFA, OSI, and ALE significantly suppressed cell migration (Figure S3D).

body.section: TP-scores of EGFR-TKIs in living H3255 cells
body.text: Collectively, all drugs displayed meaningful in vitro antitumour activity at C max concentrations, although ALE demonstrated relatively lower efficacy, as expected given the absence of ALK mutations in H3255 cells.

body.section: TP-scores of EGFR-TKIs in living H3255 cells
body.text: These results confirm the suitability of using C max for TP scoring in this model.

body.section: TP-scores of EGFR-TKIs in living H3255 cells
body.text: As shown by live-cell FRET microscopy (Figure 5A), GEF, AFA, and OSI abolished the colocalisation of CFP-EGFRL858R and YFP-GRB2, whereas ALE and GEM did not.

body.section: TP-scores of EGFR-TKIs in living H3255 cells
body.text: Correspondingly, ED -RC binding curves for GEF, AFA, and OSI exhibited downward shifts relative to DMSO-treated controls (Figure 5B).

body.section: TP-scores of EGFR-TKIs in living H3255 cells
body.text: Notably, the curves for AFA and OSI approached linearity (Figure 5B), suggesting near-complete inhibition of the EGFRL858R-GRB2 interaction by these agents.

body.section: TP-scores of EGFR-TKIs in living H3255 cells
body.text: ALE and GEM, however, produced no significant effects on this interaction (Figure 5B).

body.section: TP-scores of EGFR-TKIs in living H3255 cells
body.text: Normalised T-, P-, and TP-scores for these five drugs are summarised in Figure 5C.

body.section: TP-scores of EGFR-TKIs in living H3255 cells
body.text: The T-scores ranked highest for OSI (1.0), followed by AFA (0.84), GEF (0.57), ALE (0.05), and GEM (0.02).

body.section: TP-scores of EGFR-TKIs in living H3255 cells
body.text: GEF, AFA, and OSI showed statistically significant T-score differences compared with DMSO, reflecting substantial on-target inhibition of EGFRL858R by these agents.

body.section: TP-scores of EGFR-TKIs in living H3255 cells
body.text: Regarding P-scores, GEF ranked highest (1.0), followed by OSI (0.94), AFA (0.76), GEM (0.56), and ALE (0.49), with all five drugs producing significant phenotypic responses relative to controls.

body.section: TP-scores of EGFR-TKIs in living H3255 cells
body.text: ALE and GEM displayed relatively low T-scores (∼0.15) and moderate P-scores (∼0.5), consistent with their non-EGFR-targeted mechanisms., Finally, TP-scores ranked OSI highest (1.0), followed by AFA (0.68), GEF (0.65), ALE (0.02), and GEM (0.01).

body.section: TP-scores of EGFR-TKIs in living H3255 cells
body.text: GEF, AFA, and OSI demonstrated statistically significant TP-score differences compared with controls, with OSI exhibiting the highest TP-score and GEF the lowest.

body.section: TP-scores of EGFR-TKIs in living H3255 cells
body.text: Thus, the TP scoring system predicted greater in vivo antitumour efficacy for OSI relative to GEF in the H3255 cell model.

body.section: Validation of TP-scores in H3255 CDX models
body.text: To validate the TP-score prediction that OSI has superior in vivo antitumour efficacy compared to GEF in H3255 cells, we conducted a 21-day monotherapy study using the H3255 CDX mouse model.

body.section: Validation of TP-scores in H3255 CDX models
body.text: The doses used for GEF (51.4 mg/kg, oral gavage, QD) and OSI (16.4 mg/kg, oral gavage, QD) were based on recommended clinical dosages converted to mouse-equivalent regimens.

body.section: Validation of TP-scores in H3255 CDX models
body.text: Both GEF and OSI significantly inhibited tumour growth, with OSI demonstrating greater antitumour activity than GEF (Figure 6A-C).

body.section: Validation of TP-scores in H3255 CDX models
body.text: Neither drug caused significant changes in body weight throughout the treatment period (Figure 6I).

body.section: Validation of TP-scores in H3255 CDX models
body.text: Collectively, these findings confirm the TP-score prediction that OSI exhibits greater antitumour efficacy than GEF in vivo.

body.section: Live-cell TP scoring predicts OSI efficacy in a patient with NSCLC
body.text: We next investigated the clinical applicability of live-cell TP scoring.

body.section: Live-cell TP scoring predicts OSI efficacy in a patient with NSCLC
body.text: Considering the limited transfection efficiency and high cytotoxicity associated with plasmid-based delivery in primary cells, we optimised CFP-EGFRL858R and YFP-GRB2 into mRNA-based constructs.

body.section: Live-cell TP scoring predicts OSI efficacy in a patient with NSCLC
body.text: The structure of the mRNA-based YFP-GRB2 construct is illustrated in Figure 7A; its 5’ end was capped with CAP1 GAG, and UTP was substituted with m1Ψ to reduce immunogenicity.

body.section: Live-cell TP scoring predicts OSI efficacy in a patient with NSCLC
body.text: The mRNA-based CFP-EGFRL858R construct was similarly designed.

body.section: Live-cell TP scoring predicts OSI efficacy in a patient with NSCLC
body.text: Patient #1 (P#1) was a 43-year-old male with a suspected malignancy in the left lung who underwent surgical resection at our institution.

body.section: Live-cell TP scoring predicts OSI efficacy in a patient with NSCLC
body.text: Intraoperative frozen-section pathology confirmed invasive LUAD; consequently, fresh tumour tissue was collected, and primary tumour cells were isolated.

body.section: Live-cell TP scoring predicts OSI efficacy in a patient with NSCLC
body.text: Postoperative pathological evaluation confirmed stage IIIA LUAD (pT1bN2bM0) in the left upper lobe.

body.section: Live-cell TP scoring predicts OSI efficacy in a patient with NSCLC
body.text: Immunohistochemical results were EGFR(+), suggesting a potential EGFR mutation.

body.section: Live-cell TP scoring predicts OSI efficacy in a patient with NSCLC
body.text: Adjuvant OSI therapy is recommended for patients with resected stage IIIA NSCLC harbouring EGFR L858R or exon 19 deletion mutations.

body.section: Live-cell TP scoring predicts OSI efficacy in a patient with NSCLC
body.text: However, due to financial constraints, the patient did not undergo genetic sequencing to confirm EGFR mutation status.

body.section: Live-cell TP scoring predicts OSI efficacy in a patient with NSCLC
body.text: Given the higher prevalence of EGFR L858R mutations relative to exon 19 deletions among male patients with surgically resected stage III LUAD, we conducted EGFRL858R-GRB2 interaction-based TP scoring to evaluate this patient's potential sensitivity to OSI.

body.section: Live-cell TP scoring predicts OSI efficacy in a patient with NSCLC
body.text: Representative FRET microscopy images of living tumour cells from P#1 after 16 h of treatment with either DMSO or OSI (0.126 μM) are presented in Figure 7B.

body.section: Live-cell TP scoring predicts OSI efficacy in a patient with NSCLC
body.text: Due to substantial spontaneous fluorescence interference in the MITO fluorescence channel of primary lung tumour cells, MITO features were excluded from the clinical analysis.

body.section: Live-cell TP scoring predicts OSI efficacy in a patient with NSCLC
body.text: OSI treatment eliminated the colocalisation between CFP-EGFRL858R and YFP-GRB2 (Figure 7B), resulting in a downward shift of the FRET curves compared to control (Figure 7C).

body.section: Live-cell TP scoring predicts OSI efficacy in a patient with NSCLC
body.text: TP-score analysis (Figure 7D) demonstrated a significant increase in the T-score for OSI-treated cells; however, no significant differences were detected in the P-score or TP-score.

body.section: Live-cell TP scoring predicts OSI efficacy in a patient with NSCLC
body.text: These results indicated that while OSI effectively inhibited the EGFRL858R-GRB2 interaction in tumour cells from P#1, it failed to induce meaningful phenotypic responses, suggesting limited therapeutic benefit.

body.section: Live-cell TP scoring predicts OSI efficacy in a patient with NSCLC
body.text: This observation raised the possibility that EGFRL858R was not the oncogenic driver mutation in this patient's tumour.

body.section: Live-cell TP scoring predicts OSI efficacy in a patient with NSCLC
body.text: To clarify the low TP-score observed after OSI treatment, EGFR exons 18-21 were subsequently sequenced using the remaining patient-derived samples, because clinically actionable EGFR mutations typically occur within these exons.

body.section: Live-cell TP scoring predicts OSI efficacy in a patient with NSCLC
body.text: Alignment to the NCBI reference sequence for EGFR (NM_005228.5) confirmed the absence of clinically actionable EGFR mutations in P#1 (Figure 7E).

body.section: Live-cell TP scoring predicts OSI efficacy in a patient with NSCLC
body.text: These results explained the observed insensitivity of P#1-derived tumour cells to OSI.

body.section: Live-cell TP scoring predicts OSI efficacy in a patient with NSCLC
body.text: Taken together, live-cell TP scoring effectively predicted OSI insensitivity in this patient with NSCLC, highlighting the potential of this approach for prospectively identifying ineffective treatments.
This study provides preliminary evidence supporting the clinical feasibility of predicting EGFR-TKI efficacy by integrating the EGFRL858R-GRB2 interaction with cellular phenotype features.
The T-score, based on the EGFRL858R-GRB2 interaction, effectively assesses the on-target activity of EGFR-TKIs against EGFRL858R.
The integrated TP-score further incorporated drug-induced phenotypic responses and provided an overall prediction of EGFR-TKI efficacy.
Consequently, this TP scoring approach may support personalised EGFR-TKI selection for patients with EGFR L858R-mutant NSCLC.

The agreement between TP scoring predictions for GEF and OSI and their efficacy observed in both H3255 CDX models (Figure 6) and previously untreated patients with EGFR L858R-mutant advanced NSCLC highlights the potential utility of TP scoring in guiding precision therapy.

Although GEF and OSI showed similar cellular phenotypic responses (P-scores) in H3255 cells (Figure 5), OSI exhibited a higher T-score compared to GEF, resulting in a superior TP-score (OSI: 1.0 vs. GEF: 0.65).
These findings align with results from the CDX mouse models (Figure 6).
While maximal phenotypic inhibition was achievable by both GEF and OSI in vitro due to saturated EGFR pathway blockade.
However, the weaker antitumour activity of GEF in vivo may be attributable, at least in part, to its limited ability to maintain sustained EGFR inhibition as drug concentrations decline.

Single-cell TP scoring can distinguish drug-resistant from drug-sensitive subpopulations, facilitating targeted selection of combination therapies in heterogeneous tumours., Approximately 63%-69% of somatic mutations in renal carcinomas exhibit intratumoural regional variability, and 77% of lung cancer patients show heterogeneous EGFR expression across tumour cells.
Tumour cell heterogeneity typically confers variable sensitivity to monotherapy.

Identifying drug-resistant subpopulations within predominantly sensitive tumour populations has important clinical relevance, because combination regimens targeting both sensitive and resistant subsets may be more effective than single-agent therapy.
For instance, Alsaed et al. reported heterogeneous EGFR expression in EGFR-mutant NSCLC, identifying EGFR-low cells intrinsically resistant to OSI.
However, combining HDAC inhibitors with OSI effectively overcame this resistance.

Similarly, Hata et al. showed that combining an EGFR T790M-specific inhibitor with an apoptosis-targeting agent restored sensitivity in cells that had acquired resistance through EGFR T790M mutations.
The TP scoring procedure preserves cell viability, which may enhance its clinical practicality.
First, the short assay duration of TP scoring, approximately 16 h, compares favourably with many functional assays that require days to months.
As a result, cells remain suitable for further assays such as cell viability tests, SMPC technology, or LC-MS/MS analysis.
Combining TP scoring with additional functional assay results could further improve the accuracy of personalised treatment guidance.
Second, repeated dynamic assessments at multiple time points from the same sample may reduce variability caused by differences in the onset time of drug responses.
The live-cell TP scoring protocol aligns well with clinical workflows.
From tumour resection to final analysis, the entire assay can be completed within 48 h.

Primary tumour cells generally adhere within 24 h; combined with the subsequent 24-h TP scoring step, the entire process comfortably fits within the 10-day turnaround time recommended by clinical guidelines.
Minimising ex vivo culture duration is advantageous, as even short-term (8 days) in vitro culture can alter the therapeutic sensitivity of primary tumour cells.

Additionally, employing clinically relevant maximal plasma drug concentrations (C max) in live-cell TP scoring ensures the translational validity of the observed responses by closely simulating maximal in vivo tumour exposure.,
Further improvements in P-score sensitivity may be achieved by incorporating unsupervised deep-learning approaches for single-cell phenotypic analysis.
The low OSI P-score observed in P#1 was consistent with the absence of actionable EGFR mutations.
However, the current supervised CellProfiler- and LDA-based analysis may have limited sensitivity for detecting subtle drug-induced phenotypic changes.
Recent unsupervised deep-learning methods, such as MorphoGenie and PhenoProfiler, have shown superior phenotypic discrimination compared with conventional machine-learning approaches.

In evaluations using a large-scale dataset comprising nearly 400 000 high-content images and more than 8 million single-cell images, PhenoProfiler consistently outperformed existing methods, with improvements in accuracy and robustness of up to 20%.
Three-dimensional (3D) models represent an ideal platform for future clinical translation of the TP scoring.
The two-dimensional (2D) cultures of patient-derived tumour cells used in this study do not fully recapitulate the in vivo tumour microenvironment.

Previous applications of FRET and HCS in 3D models support the feasibility of extending our platform to 3D models., Anand et al. used a FRET-based biosensor to monitor paclitaxel-induced apoptosis in a 3D breast tumour model, and Koedoot et al. developed an ex vivo, HCS-based 3D microtumour platform to predict changes in target lesions and PFS in response to platinum-based chemotherapy in patients with ovarian cancer.

In summary, our findings support the feasibility of integrating the EGFRL858R-GRB2 interaction and cellular phenotype assessment through live-cell FRET microscopy as a predictive approach for evaluating EGFR-TKI efficacy.

Further studies are required to establish the capability of TP scoring in discriminating heterogeneous tumour cell populations, as well as its practical applicability and predictive accuracy in clinical settings.
Ultimately, we anticipate that TP scoring can contribute meaningfully to personalised treatment decisions for cancer patients, thus minimising unnecessary exposure to ineffective therapies.
